It's the 23rd of December 2031, in Sibiu. Lena is in the kitchen with Mrs Elena Ionescu, Andrei and Mara's mother. Since the summer she met Lena, she has been taking German lessons. Andrei translates when needed.
Lena, today I'll show you the recipe for cozonac. My mother showed it to me forty years ago in this kitchen.
It's a great honour. Andrei has often told me about your cozonac in Berlin.
Has he? He's never told me he misses it. He rings me every Sunday and just says: everything's fine, Mum.
Mum, I've told you that a thousand times already.
No. You've never told me. You only showed me, by coming home every year at Christmas. Except last year.
Last year was the opening of my café. He stayed in Berlin because of me. I'm sorry.
You don't have to be sorry. You're here now. And now we knead the dough together, for half an hour, by hand, not with the machine.
Half an hour? Andrei, why didn't you tell me that? In my café I knead the dough with the machine.
Because I knew Mum would rather show you herself.
He's right. Some things you don't learn from books. You learn them in a warm kitchen, from an old woman with flour on her hands.
For kneading I'm old enough. Come on, give me the flour. And you can give me the butter afterwards.
Germans pronounce it “KO-tso-nak”; you know how to say it properly: in Romanian it's “ko-zo-NAHK”!
1. TeKaMoLo: the order of the adverbials
When you have several pieces of information in the middle of the sentence, the natural order is: Temporal (when) – Kausal (why) – Modal (how) – Lokal (where / where to).
Yesterday, because of the snow, we went to Sibiu by night train.
You don't have to use all four. But the order stays the same: “Ich fahre morgen mit dem Bus zur Arbeit.” (Te – Mo – Lo)
Any element can move to first position for emphasis: “Wegen des Schnees sind wir gestern mit dem Nachtzug gefahren.”
Ich gebe meiner Mutter das Buch.
Ich gebe es meiner Mutter. / Ich gebe ihr das Buch.
Quick rule: short pronouns come early. Of two pronouns, “es / ihn / sie” (accusative) comes before “mir / dir / ihr” (dative).
Negating the whole sentence: “nicht” goes as far towards the end as possible, but before the participle, the infinitive, the separable prefix and phrases of place / direction:
Negating one part: “nicht” goes right before the element being negated, often with “sondern”:
I don't knead with the machine, but by hand.
It wasn't Andrei who called, but his mother.

They had left on the evening of the twenty-first of December on the night train from Berlin via Budapest to Sibiu. The journey had taken twenty-four hours, and because of the snow in Hungary, twenty-six. Lena had barely slept all night in the narrow bunk of the sleeping car. She had looked out of the window as the lights of the villages went by and wondered whether Andrei's mother would like her. Andrei had slept in the upper bunk like a child going home.

Sibiu was white and quiet when they arrived. The snow lay on the roofs of the old houses in the centre, on the church towers, on the branches of the trees in the park. Elena and Dan were standing on the platform, she a small woman in a navy-blue coat, with a hat she had knitted herself, he tall and silent, his left arm still in a sling. Elena hugged her son first, for a long time, without saying anything. Then she looked at Lena and said, slowly and carefully, in German, with a strong accent: “Welcome back, Lena. I have learned German. For you. You are too thin. We will change that.” Lena was so surprised that tears came to her eyes. Last summer Elena hadn't spoken a word of German.

Dan gave Lena his good hand and said just one word, in Romanian: “Bine.” (“Good.”) Andrei explained to her later that, coming from his father, this meant about as much as a long speech from other people. Then Dan picked up Lena's heavy suitcase with his good hand, and when Andrei wanted to help him, he just shook his head. A man with a broken arm still carries his guest's suitcase. That's how it was in Sibiu.

The Ionescu family's house was in the Lower Town, an old house with thick walls and a garden where everything was now sleeping under the snow. Inside it was small, warm and full of things: books, photos, rugs on the walls, crocheted blankets on every armchair. In the living room stood a Christmas tree that Elena had decorated with old glass baubles, some as old as Andrei, some older. And everywhere there was a smell of food. Lena had never eaten as much in her life as in those first three days in Sibiu: sarmale (cabbage rolls), ciorbă (sour soup), salată de boeuf (a Romanian potato and meat salad), and cozonac again and again.

On the second day Dan took Lena out into the garden, to the beehives standing under a thick layer of snow. He spoke Romanian, slowly, and Andrei translated. “The bees aren't really sleeping now,” said Dan. “They all stay together in a cluster, with the queen in the middle, and shiver their wings to stay warm. The bees on the edge freeze, then they go inside, and others come out to the edge. All winter long. None of them stays out in the cold all the time.” He looked at Lena, then at his son. “It's the same with a family,” he said. Andrei didn't translate the last sentence straight away. He had to clear his throat first.

Lena and Elena made themselves understood with gestures. Elena's German was the German of a six-month evening class, full of textbook words. Lena's Romanian consisted of exactly twenty words, which she had learned in the summer and had since almost all forgotten. But in the kitchen they didn't need an interpreter. Kneading the dough, rolling the sarmale, washing up afterwards, they understood each other without many words. Andrei sometimes came into the kitchen, saw the two women laughing and went out again without asking why.

On the morning of the twenty-fourth of December, Andrei took Lena by the hand and led her down through the snowy garden to a small wooden shed at the end of the garden. He opened the padlock with an old key that he had been carrying in his wallet for three years. “My grandfather's workshop,” he said. “Since his funeral I haven't had the courage to go in.”

Inside it was cold and dark and smelled of wood and oil. Tools hung on the walls, neatly side by side, each in its place: saws, planes, chisels, hammers of every size. There was dust on the workbench, and under the dust was a piece of wood, half carved. Lena went closer. It was a little bird, a robin maybe, with finished wings and a head that was still just a rough block.
Every winter he carved a bird for my grandmother. Fifty-one years, one every Christmas. They're all in Mum's cupboard. He never finished this one. He died in November, six weeks before Christmas.

Lena looked at the bird, then at Andrei, then at the tools on the wall. And suddenly she understood something she hadn't understood in three years in Berlin: why Andrei got up every morning at four and baked bread, by hand, slowly, without complaining. Why he wrote stories in a brown notebook. Why he never talked about feelings but was always making something. He was the grandson of a man who had carved his love into wood for fifty-one years.
Finish it. The bird. Here, now, before we go back. For your mother.
I haven't carved anything for ten years. He showed me when I was a child, but I was never any good.
You knead dough by hand every day. You can do it. I'll wait for you.

And Andrei took a small knife from the wall, sat down on his grandfather's old stool and began, very slowly, to carve the bird's head. Lena sat down on a crate in the corner, wrapped herself in her jacket and watched him. Outside it was snowing again. It took four hours. Her feet got cold, her fingers went stiff, but she didn't go into the house. When Andrei finally finished, the bird had a head, a little beak and two slightly crooked eyes. But it looked as if it were about to sing.

On Christmas Eve, after dinner, Andrei handed his mother a little parcel wrapped in newspaper. Elena opened it slowly. When she saw the bird, she said nothing for a long time. Then she stood up, went to the cupboard and put it next to the others, fifty-one wooden birds in a long row. The fifty-second stood right at the end, a little crooked, a little different from the others.
Now the row is complete. He would have laughed at the eyes. But he would have been proud. Very proud.

Dan had sat silently at the table the whole time. Now he stood up, fetched a big jar of honey from the pantry, golden and dark, and put it on the table in front of Lena. On the label, in his big, unpractised handwriting, in German, with two mistakes, it said: “Für der Kaffee Bei Ingrid. Von Dan.” (“For the café Bei Ingrid. From Dan.”) Lena read it and laughed and cried at the same time, and she didn't correct the mistakes. She hugged the big, silent man carefully, because of his arm, and he patted her twice on the back, the way you do with a child you love. Later Andrei told her that his father had practised writing those seven words every evening for two weeks.

Late in the evening Andrei's phone rang. It was a video call from Berlin. On the small screen you could see Ludwig's living room, the Christmas tree, Mara, still in her hospital clothes, Jakob, Kuba and Ola, and Ludwig himself, with a red hat on his head that someone had obviously put on him against his will. “Merry Christmas to Romania!” they all shouted. And Ludwig leaned towards the camera and said something he had obviously practised for a long time, in Romanian so bad that Elena cried with laughter: “Crăciun fericit, doamna Ionescu! Mulțumesc pentru Mara și Andrei!” (“Merry Christmas, Mrs Ionescu! Thank you for Mara and Andrei!”)
